canonical_statement: The study tests whether well-resourced frontier AI agents can conduct novel, open-ended AI research on uncontaminated research questions.
A shadow evaluation gives an agent the central research question from a high-quality unpublished paper and has the original paper authors grade the agent output as a conference submission.
The primary evaluation used two unpublished NeurIPS 2026 submissions, one on LLM persona structure/control and one on distribution-shift detection for tabular prior-fitted networks.
Original paper authors formulated the research questions without revealing promising solution paths, helped set resource budgets, and graded the finished agent papers.
Both main experiments used Claude Opus 4.8 with extra-high reasoning in the OpenClaw scaffold.

concept.text: Claude Opus 4.8 with extra-high reasoning on OpenClaw

canonical_statement: Main-run agents received a Linux VM in AWS, access to the open web, GPU resources, API-budget monitoring, deadline monitoring, subagent delegation, and a persistent research log.
Agents had a blind self-review subagent plus access to the Stanford Agentic Reviewer, CMU Paper Reviewer, and refine.ink for external AI review.
The researchers restricted scaffold modifications to changes intended to apply to machine-learning research generally rather than to either target research question.
The main runs required three categories of human intervention: patching an OpenClaw reasoning-model bug, granting a 24-hour extension, and requesting a final rewrite for accessibility.
Twelve collaborators completed a pre-experiment expectations survey before results were shared.

canonical_statement: Across the study there were five agent runs: two pilot runs without reasoning, two main runs with extra-high reasoning using OpenClaw and Opus 4.8, and one Codex/GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra robustness run.
The highest-bar outcome was whether the original authors would rate the agent-generated paper at least a weak accept at a top-tier AI conference.
A moderate success criterion was answering the research question in a novel and defensible or reviewer-impressing way even if the finished paper was not acceptable.
The Personas research question asked whether LLM personas can be decomposed, measured, and controlled as positions in a structured trait space using weight-space interventions.

The TabPFN research question asked for a theoretically justified, empirically validated deployment-time detector that alarms when deployment accuracy is materially worse than in-distribution accuracy using white-box PFN access and unlabeled deployment data.
The original-author review score for the Personas agent paper on quality was 2/4.

canonical_statement: AI reviews often identified concerns similar to the human experts, but the agents failed to prioritize the most consequential critiques and instead narrowed claims or added caveats.
Because both evaluated papers were rejects, the study cannot determine whether AI reviewers were accurately discriminating research quality or merely tending to reject all drafts.

Agents successfully completed the research-engineering prerequisites, including literature review, GPU debugging, large experiment batches, web/email review retrieval, and full LaTeX paper compilation.
Nine of eleven survey respondents expected a loop of unresolvable errors, but the main agents resolved all environmental barriers except one OpenClaw bug that humans patched.

canonical_statement: Two no-reasoning Opus 4.8 pilot runs showed the same broad failure modes as the main runs but had poorer literature review and substantially worse writing.
The authors judged the no-reasoning pilot outputs too weak to warrant external review by the original paper authors.
A Claude Fable 5 attempt to improve the scaffold from pilot logs made broad rule changes based on an n=1 example and did not appear to address the fundamental failure modes.

Log analysis identified poor judgment about the bar for high-quality research: agents used underpowered synthetic or hand-picked evidence and settled on research directions before the evidence warranted it.
Agents generated plausible initial hypotheses but showed weak creative problem solving once those hypotheses failed, tending to narrow claims instead of redesigning the research approach.
Agents backtracked locally by rerunning experiments or adding robustness checks but did not restart the project-level approach after repeated negative reviews.

In the TabPFN run, six distinct approaches were considered and falsified within the first fourteen hours, after which the solution approach was not fundamentally revised despite about 110 hours remaining to the original deadline.

concept.text: Claude Opus 4.8 with extra-high reasoning on OpenClaw - TabPFN run

canonical_statement: Both agents showed poor context and resource awareness: they could query token, compute, and time budgets yet left large fractions unused and sometimes stopped while time remained.

The agents exhibited instruction drift over multi-day runs, including failure to consistently use refine.ink, violations of paper/abstract length limits, and disregard of exploration-time rules acknowledged earlier.
The robustness check reran the TabPFN task using GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex at an ultra reasoning level and a recurring loop that resumed work after budget checks and model-generated NeurIPS review.
The GPT-5.6 Sol/Codex robustness run reproduced major failures: underpowered experiments, no novel contribution, misformatted figures, missing appendices, and ineffective budget management.
The GPT-5.6 Sol/Codex robustness run exhausted a $3,000 token-usage budget in just over two days, leaving nearly 100 hours of allotted wall-clock time.

concept.text: Token-budget depletion relative to wall-clock budget

canonical_statement: The robustness run also reproduced positive behaviors: AI self-review continued to reject weak drafts, hypotheses were registered, negative findings were reported instead of fabricated positives, and the agent used a real-world shifted dataset.
The evaluation has a very small sample: two target research questions, four OpenClaw/Opus pilot or main runs, and one GPT-5.6 Sol/Codex robustness run.
Original-author grading was not blind: reviewers had authored the source research and knew the evaluated papers were AI-generated, creating potential reviewer bias.
Question selection involved researcher discretion and may not generalize to incremental AI research or to AI R&D work that can be optimized against well-specified objectives.
Evaluation awareness may have affected agent behavior because agents were explicitly told they were being evaluated against a NeurIPS review rubric.
OpenClaw had a reasoning-model session-reset bug that caused 14 resets in the TabPFN run and 5 in the Personas run, with each reset losing accumulated context.
The authors could not test Anthropic Fable/Mythos 5 because frontier AI R&D capabilities were access-limited.

The agents had six days, whereas the original researchers spent substantially longer and used more GPU compute; the authors argue this likely does not explain the principal failures but cannot eliminate the constraint.

The authors state that the core teams prior skepticism about imminent recursive self-improvement could have influenced question selection, evaluation design, log interpretation, and the labeling of observed failure modes.
The causal interpretation of the observed failures is contested within the author group; alternatives include lack of creativity, poor judgment, reasoning/logic deficits, and epistemic lock-in.

The authors interpret the study as preliminary evidence that current frontier agents can perform the engineering of AI research but are not yet capable of autonomously conducting some open-ended AI research at top-conference quality.

The authors caution that failure on the studied open-ended tasks does not establish that AI agents cannot accelerate AI R&D, because full automation of such tasks may not lie on the critical path to acceleration.
The project reports funding from Coefficient Giving and Schmidt Sciences, with OpenAI providing API credits for GPT-5.6 Sol evaluation.
The authors release expert reviews, survey responses, agent repositories, and run logs, but note that detailed logs and the generated paper for one not-yet-public target paper are not disclosed.

The authors disclose AI assistance for LaTeX conversion, reference formatting, copyediting, coding assistance, AI-assisted log analysis, and table/figure editing, and state that AI outputs were verified at each phase.
In the pre-experiment survey, seven of twelve respondents identified creativity and judgment as the expected proximate cause if the agent failed the highest success bar.
